story_candidates.hed: Wazn — the Dove's orange giant that will not stay put
story_candidates.dek: Two bright stars draw the back of Columba, the Dove. They seem to travel together across the winter sky, but the pairing is an illusion of perspective. Wazn, the warmer-coloured member, is a nearby evolved star whose measured motion will slowly alter the familiar pattern.
story_candidates.body:
Wazn is Beta Columbae (β Col), HD 39425, HIP 27628 and HR 2040, permanent Star Almanack object 772. The International Astronomical Union approved the name *Wazn* for Beta Columbae on 20 July 2016. Its visual magnitude is about 3.1, making it the second-brightest star of Columba after Phact, Alpha Columbae. The name comes from Arabic *al-wazn*, “the weight.” These identifiers all describe the same star; the Beta letter is part of a historical naming system, not a physical ranking of stellar mass.

Wazn is not a hot blue star like Phact. Its spectrum is classified K1 III, with some catalogues appending **CN+1**. K indicates a cooler orange photosphere, and III marks a giant: a star that has expanded after its long main-sequence phase. The CN notation describes a feature of molecular absorption bands in the observed spectrum; it does not mean that a giant is made mostly of cyanogen. A commonly quoted effective temperature is about 4,500 kelvin. Spectral class, temperature and chemical-band strength are related but not interchangeable measurements.

The star is comparatively close. A Hipparcos parallax of 37.41 ± 0.12 milliarcseconds gives about 26.7 parsecs, or 87 light-years, by straightforward inversion. Gaia-based estimates differ slightly depending on data release and inference method; the sensible statement for a visual guide is “roughly 87–90 light-years,” not a distance exact to the last decimal. The light in tonight's eyepiece left Wazn decades before many present-day observers were born.

Its motion is a better surprise. Catalogued proper motion is about 55 milliarcseconds per year in right ascension (including the cosine-of-declination convention) and 404 milliarcseconds per year in declination. Combined, these are about 0.41 arcseconds per year, or roughly 41 arcseconds in a century. That is far too slow to notice during an observing session but large enough for precise astrometry and long-baseline photographic comparisons. The radial velocity, about +89 kilometres per second, also indicates substantial motion away from the Sun along our line of sight. Proper motion and radial velocity measure different components of space motion; neither is the star's speed across the celestial sphere expressed in kilometres per second without its distance.

Phact and Wazn have almost the same right ascension and stand only a few degrees apart in our sky, so older star lore often treated them as a pair. Richard Hinckley Allen's nineteenth-century compilation associates the two with Arabic group names including *Al Muhlifain*, though such historical names and translations should not be mistaken for present-day official designations. Wazn's nearby distance and evolved orange spectrum contrast with Phact's much hotter B-type spectrum. A constellation figure is a useful pattern on the sky, not proof of a gravitational family.

To locate Wazn, first find Orion and bright Sirius, then look south into Columba. Phact is the brighter, bluer of the conspicuous pair; Wazn is slightly fainter and lies a little farther east and south. Verify both against the accepted Dove figure and the object's finder rather than relying on perceived colour alone. The J2000 position of Wazn is approximately right ascension 5h 50m 58s and declination −35° 46′. At 45° N its ideal upper-culmination altitude is only about 9.2°, making haze, terrain and city light severe limitations. At 35° S it passes about 89.2° high, nearly overhead. These are original geometric calculations that ignore refraction and the observing date.

A small telescope resolves no stellar surface; binoculars mainly help with the surrounding pattern. The real experiment is to compare two stars of the Dove while remembering that their different temperatures, distances and motions make them separate worlds. The week's Moon, twilight, finder rendering and published links must be checked independently before this story can be marked complete.

## Sources

- [IAU star-name catalogue](https://iauarchive.eso.org/public/themes/naming_stars/); [Wazn's historical name](https://www.constellationsofwords.com/wazn/)

- [SIMBAD identifier search for Beta Columbae](https://simbad.u-strasbg.fr/simbad/sim-id?Ident=bet+Col); [compiled stellar measurements](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beta_Columbae)

- [Hipparcos astrometry summary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beta_Columbae); [Gaia-linked measurements and provenance](https://asteriastar.com/stars/wazn)

- [astrometric and spectroscopic data compilation](https://asteriastar.com/stars/wazn)

- [Allen's historical compilation](https://www.constellationsofwords.com/wazn/); [Phact and Columba](https://www.constellation-guide.com/constellation-list/columba-constellation/)

story_candidates.hed: M37: The Auriga Open Cluster in the Night Sky
story_candidates.dek: A prominent stellar group within Auriga, offering a captivating glimpse of stellar youth and galactic structure.
story_candidates.body:
M37, also known as Messier 37, is a striking open cluster nestled within the constellation Auriga. Recognized for its richness and relatively young age, this celestial assembly offers astronomers and stargazers an excellent opportunity to observe the collective beauty of stars born from the same molecular cloud. Situated approximately 4,500 light-years from Earth, M37 comprises several hundred stars, many of which are bright enough to be seen with binoculars or small telescopes, making it accessible to amateur astronomers.

This open cluster spans roughly 20 light-years across and is estimated to be around 300 million years old, placing it among the younger stellar groups in our galaxy. Its dense core contains a multitude of stars, with some residents shining more brightly than our Sun. The cluster's stars are loosely bound by mutual gravitational attraction, which over time, may lead to their dispersion into the Milky Way's disk.

M37's position in Auriga makes it a prominent feature during winter and early spring in the northern hemisphere, offering a spectacular sight away from city lights. The cluster's location near the bright star Capella provides an easy reference point for locating it in the night sky. Observers often enjoy tracking the changing appearance of M37 as telescopic magnification reveals its varying stellar constituents and the hints of its evolutionary state.

As a physical object candidate, M37 exemplifies the dynamic and ever-changing nature of our galaxy's stellar populations. Observations of such clusters help astronomers understand star formation processes and the lifecycle of star groups in the Milky Way. Whether viewed through binoculars or telescopes, M37 remains a compelling target that vividly illustrates the beauty and complexity of our cosmic neighborhood.

story_candidates.hed: Betelgeuse: A Red Supergiant in Orion's Winter Cross
story_candidates.dek: Illuminating the night sky with its distinctive hue, Betelgeuse stands as a beacon of stellar evolution and celestial wonder.
story_candidates.body:
Betelgeuse, designated as Alpha Orionis, is one of the most prominent stars in the night sky, renowned for its striking reddish hue and its role as a key component of the Winter Triangle asterism. Situated in the constellation Orion, this star is classified as a red supergiant, marking it as an evolved, massive star nearing the end of its life cycle. Its coordinates are approximately right ascension 5.92 hours and declination +7.41 degrees, making it a conspicuous feature in the winter sky for northern hemisphere observers.

Betelgeuse’s luminosity is significantly greater than that of our Sun, with its brightness often varying due to pulsations inherent in its stellar structure. Its size and mass are immense, with a radius roughly hundreds of times greater than the Sun’s, though its exact measurements can be challenging to determine precisely because of its variability and distance. Despite these measurement complexities, Betelgeuse remains a star of keen scientific interest, especially regarding the late evolutionary stages of massive stars.

Its role as a figure star in celestial navigation and star mapping accentuates its importance in both historical and contemporary astronomy. Betelgeuse’s distinctive reddish appearance makes it an easily identifiable marker in the winter sky, a key part of the Orion constellation and the Winter Triangle asterism. As a bright star with a notable red hue, it serves as a celestial lighthouse, guiding observers and astronomers alike.

Understanding Betelgeuse contributes to broader insights into stellar lifecycle processes, such as supernova precursors, given it is expected to eventually explode, though this event remains unpredictable on human timescales. As it continues to evolve, Betelgeuse will likely remain a subject of fascination and study, inspiring generations of skywatchers and scientific inquiry.

story_candidates.hed: Menkalinan: A Prominent Bright Star in the Constellation Aquarius
story_candidates.dek: An overview of Menkalinan, its characteristics, and its significance in the night sky.
story_candidates.body:
Menkalinan, also known by its Bayer designation Beta Aurigae, is one of the notable bright stars situated in the constellation Auriga. Located at approximately 5.99 hours right ascension and around 44.95 degrees declination, Menkalinan is prominent in the northern celestial hemisphere. Its brightness makes it a key object for stargazers and astronomers alike, serving as a navigational beacon and a fixture of celestial navigation throughout history.

This star is classified as a stellar object candidate with notable brightness, appearing brighter than many other stars in the night sky, which categorizes it among the more luminous in its region. Its inclusion in star catalogs, such as the Hipparcos and Bayer star lists, underscores its significance and the ease with which it can be identified in the sky.

Menkalinan is believed to be a complex star system, possibly comprising multiple stars that appear as a single point of light to the naked eye. Its apparent magnitude and position make it a conspicuous figure in the constellation Auriga, often utilized for orientation and educational purposes in astronomical observations.

The star's precise coordinates have been recorded in various stellar catalogs, with measurements aligning around right ascension 5.992 degrees and declination approximately 44.95 degrees. These coordinates facilitate accurate tracking and study, which is essential for long-term observational projects and for amateurs aiming to locate it in the sky.

In the grand tapestry of the night sky, Menkalinan is more than just a bright point; it is a stable, guiding light that connects us to the broader universe. Its characteristics continue to stimulate study and admiration, ensuring its place in the enduring field of astronomical observation and stargazing traditions.

story_candidates.hed: M35: A Brilliant Gem in Gemini's Sky
story_candidates.dek: An enduring open cluster that captivates stargazers with its youthful glow and intricate structure.
story_candidates.body:
Located in the constellation Gemini, M35 is a prominent open star cluster that has long been a favorite among astronomers and amateur stargazers alike. Situated at a right ascension of approximately 6.15 hours and a declination of about +24.33 degrees, this cluster offers a splendid view of numerous bright stars spread over an expansive region of the night sky. M35’s apparent brightness and rich stellar content make it a compelling target for observers equipped with modest telescopes, revealing a glittering assembly of young stars that are believed to have formed from the same molecular cloud.

Open clusters like M35 are vital for understanding stellar evolution because they contain stars of roughly the same age and chemical composition. This particular cluster is estimated to be several hundred million years old, showcasing the vibrant blue hues of its hot, young stars. Its distance from Earth is typically placed around 2,800 light-years, allowing us to glimpse it as it was hundreds of millennia ago, a reminder of the vast timescales involved in cosmic scales.

M35 is not only a spectacular sight but also an important object of study for astronomers trying to piece together the history of our galaxy. Its membership includes a mixture of bright, easily observable stars and fainter members that require more detailed observation to identify. The cluster’s structure exhibits a loosely bound assemblage of stars, indicating that it is in the process of dispersing over time due to gravitational interactions.

For observers, M35 offers a window into stellar formation and evolution, highlighting the dynamic and ongoing processes that shape our universe. Whether viewed through binoculars or a small telescope, this celestial jewel continues to inspire fascination and curiosity, connecting us with the grand tapestry of the cosmos.

story_candidates.hed: Alpha Men: A Bright Beacon in the Southern Sky
story_candidates.dek: An overview of Alpha Men, a notable star in the constellation Men, highlighting its significance and characteristics.
story_candidates.body:
Alpha Men, also catalogued as Alpha Mensae, is a prominent star situated in the constellation Men, a less conspicuous constellation in the southern celestial hemisphere. With a right ascension of approximately 6.17 hours and a declination of about -74.75 degrees, it occupies a notable position that makes it a key reference point for astronomers and stargazers alike.

As a star, Alpha Men plays a vital role in the celestial landscape of the southern sky. Its designation as 'Alpha' indicates its status as the brightest star within its constellation, a common nomenclature in traditional astronomy. Though not as luminous as some of the more famous celestial giants, Alpha Men holds observational interest due to its intrinsic properties and its role as a navigational landmark.

The characteristics of Alpha Men serve as a fascinating example of stellar diversity. While specific details of its magnitude or spectral type are subject to ongoing studies and observations, stars like Alpha Men typically range across various classifications that inform us about their temperature, size, and stage of stellar evolution. Such stars often serve as benchmarks for understanding stellar processes and the life cycle of stars.

In addition to its scientific importance, Alpha Men contributes to the cultural tapestry of sky lore and navigation. Its position and visibility make it a useful marker for southward navigation, particularly in regions where more prominent stars are not observed as easily.

Overall, Alpha Men remains a point of interest that embodies the ongoing quest to understand our universe. Its position, brightness, and role within the constellation Men ensure that it retains a lasting significance both in celestial mapping and in the collective fascination with the night sky.

story_candidates.hed: Exploring Collinder 87: A Distinguished Open Cluster in Orion
story_candidates.dek: An overview of the characteristics and significance of Collinder 87 within the constellation Orion.
story_candidates.body:
Collinder 87 is an intriguing open cluster nestled within the constellation Orion, one of the most prominent and recognizable constellations in the night sky. This stellar assembly is classified as an open cluster, a type of celestial grouping that consists of young stars loosely bound by mutual gravitational attraction. Situated at a right ascension of approximately 6.2292 hours and a declination of +12.8067 degrees, Collinder 87 can be observed as a faint, diffuse grouping of stars when viewed with suitable telescopic equipment.

Open clusters such as Collinder 87 serve as important laboratories for astronomers seeking to understand star formation and stellar evolution. These clusters typically contain stars that formed from the same molecular cloud and are thus roughly the same age, offering a unique window into the processes that influence stellar development. Although specific details about the age, distance, or individual stellar members of Collinder 87 are not comprehensively established, its classification as a physical object candidate suggests ongoing interest and study within the astronomical community.

The constellation Orion provides a stunning celestial backdrop for viewing Collinder 87, especially given Orion's prominence and the ease of locating it in the winter sky of the northern hemisphere. Observers with modest telescopes can often glimpses parts of the cluster, while larger instruments reveal a more detailed structure of its stellar population. Because it is cataloged among the prominent entries in the finest New General Catalog (NGC) listings, Collinder 87 holds a place of interest for both amateur astronomers and professional researchers interested in the dynamic processes of star clustering.

In summary, Collinder 87 remains an object of interest within the broader context of galactic structure studies. Its position in Orion and its classification as an open cluster make it a notable feature for those exploring the celestial tapestry, whether for scientific inquiry or for the aesthetic enjoyment of the night sky.

stories.hed: Wazn — the Dove's orange giant that will not stay put
stories.dek: Two bright stars draw the back of Columba, the Dove. They seem to travel together across the winter sky, but the pairing is an illusion of perspective. Wazn, the warmer-coloured member, is a nearby evolved star whose measured motion will slowly alter the familiar pattern.
stories.body:
Wazn is Beta Columbae (β Col), HD 39425, HIP 27628 and HR 2040, permanent Star Almanack object 772. The International Astronomical Union approved the name *Wazn* for Beta Columbae on 20 July 2016. Its visual magnitude is about 3.1, making it the second-brightest star of Columba after Phact, Alpha Columbae. The name comes from Arabic *al-wazn*, “the weight.” These identifiers all describe the same star; the Beta letter is part of a historical naming system, not a physical ranking of stellar mass.

Wazn is not a hot blue star like Phact. Its spectrum is classified K1 III, with some catalogues appending **CN+1**. K indicates a cooler orange photosphere, and III marks a giant: a star that has expanded after its long main-sequence phase. The CN notation describes a feature of molecular absorption bands in the observed spectrum; it does not mean that a giant is made mostly of cyanogen. A commonly quoted effective temperature is about 4,500 kelvin. Spectral class, temperature and chemical-band strength are related but not interchangeable measurements.

The star is comparatively close. A Hipparcos parallax of 37.41 ± 0.12 milliarcseconds gives about 26.7 parsecs, or 87 light-years, by straightforward inversion. Gaia-based estimates differ slightly depending on data release and inference method; the sensible statement for a visual guide is “roughly 87–90 light-years,” not a distance exact to the last decimal. The light in tonight's eyepiece left Wazn decades before many present-day observers were born.

Its motion is a better surprise. Catalogued proper motion is about 55 milliarcseconds per year in right ascension (including the cosine-of-declination convention) and 404 milliarcseconds per year in declination. Combined, these are about 0.41 arcseconds per year, or roughly 41 arcseconds in a century. That is far too slow to notice during an observing session but large enough for precise astrometry and long-baseline photographic comparisons. The radial velocity, about +89 kilometres per second, also indicates substantial motion away from the Sun along our line of sight. Proper motion and radial velocity measure different components of space motion; neither is the star's speed across the celestial sphere expressed in kilometres per second without its distance.

Phact and Wazn have almost the same right ascension and stand only a few degrees apart in our sky, so older star lore often treated them as a pair. Richard Hinckley Allen's nineteenth-century compilation associates the two with Arabic group names including *Al Muhlifain*, though such historical names and translations should not be mistaken for present-day official designations. Wazn's nearby distance and evolved orange spectrum contrast with Phact's much hotter B-type spectrum. A constellation figure is a useful pattern on the sky, not proof of a gravitational family.

To locate Wazn, first find Orion and bright Sirius, then look south into Columba. Phact is the brighter, bluer of the conspicuous pair; Wazn is slightly fainter and lies a little farther east and south. Verify both against the accepted Dove figure and the object's finder rather than relying on perceived colour alone. The J2000 position of Wazn is approximately right ascension 5h 50m 58s and declination −35° 46′. At 45° N its ideal upper-culmination altitude is only about 9.2°, making haze, terrain and city light severe limitations. At 35° S it passes about 89.2° high, nearly overhead. These are original geometric calculations that ignore refraction and the observing date.

A small telescope resolves no stellar surface; binoculars mainly help with the surrounding pattern. The real experiment is to compare two stars of the Dove while remembering that their different temperatures, distances and motions make them separate worlds. The week's Moon, twilight, finder rendering and published links must be checked independently before this story can be marked complete.

## Sources

- [IAU star-name catalogue](https://iauarchive.eso.org/public/themes/naming_stars/); [Wazn's historical name](https://www.constellationsofwords.com/wazn/)

- [SIMBAD identifier search for Beta Columbae](https://simbad.u-strasbg.fr/simbad/sim-id?Ident=bet+Col); [compiled stellar measurements](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beta_Columbae)

- [Hipparcos astrometry summary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beta_Columbae); [Gaia-linked measurements and provenance](https://asteriastar.com/stars/wazn)

- [astrometric and spectroscopic data compilation](https://asteriastar.com/stars/wazn)

- [Allen's historical compilation](https://www.constellationsofwords.com/wazn/); [Phact and Columba](https://www.constellation-guide.com/constellation-list/columba-constellation/)

Whether viewed through binoculars or telescopes, M37 remains a compelling target that vividly illustrates the beauty and complexity of our cosmic neighborhood.
